criteria.name: Character-specific voice
criteria.instruction: Score whether diction, rhythm, figurative language, and attitude create a distinctive voice appropriate to the character or narrator. Score high when the voice remains controlled and individualized; score low when it is generic or depends on one repeated verbal gimmick.
criteria.rationale: R15 sustains an arch satirical voice, and R36 makes customer-service jargon feel characterful within its fantasy setting. R08 and R21 instead rely heavily on repetitive stoner or surfer speech without comparable development.

criteria.name: Form mirrors content
criteria.instruction: Score high if the story's structural or formal choice (fragmented syntax, found-document framing, list format, verse, unusual punctuation, tense/person choice) is itself an expressive device that enacts or reinforces the story's central idea, rather than being a neutral default container for the plot. Score low if the prose form is generic past-tense narration with no relationship between how it's told and what it's about.
criteria.rationale: R17's stuttering, miscounted sentences ('1, 2, 3. 1, 2, 3... 24. Sorry. 24.') formally enact the time-loop's disorientation; R09's in-universe 'Containment Protocol' extract framing suits its documentary-history concept; R29's clipped, ellipsis-heavy lines mirror the narrator's chemically numbed affect. None of these would score on a checklist that only asks 'is the prose competent.'

criteria.name: Beats escalate; the situation becomes irreversible
criteria.instruction: Track the story's beats in order and ask whether each one changes the situation. CLEARLY SATISFYING: pressure compounds -- new information, new cost, or a closed-off option at each turn -- so that by the end something cannot be undone. CLEARLY FAILING: the same beat repeats with variation but no increase (a gag performed three or four times at the same intensity), or events occur and leave the world exactly as it was found. A story may be static by design if the stasis is the subject, but then the stasis must be doing work the reader can name.
criteria.rationale: R12 escalates from a defensive war story to a confession to an appetite; R34 raises the cost of the hatching with each death and ends the narrator locked into a life they dread; R02 tightens from a flickering lamp to a body to a message. Against these, R13 stages the same wall-licking joke four times at identical intensity while the emotional description grows louder rather than the situation changing, and R09 and R26 both end where they began. Repetition with escalating adjectives reads as rising action to a per-item judge; it is not.

criteria.name: Fresh handling of a familiar trope
criteria.instruction: Score high if the story takes a well-worn genre trope (monster under the bed, thought-experiment classroom scene, curse reversal, etc.) and complicates, subverts, or extends it in a way a reader wouldn't already expect. Score low if the trope is executed exactly as genre convention predicts, with no additional turn.
criteria.rationale: R01's big-sister-defeats-the-closet-monster is a competently executed but wholly conventional rendition of its trope with no surprise in how it resolves. R40 instead takes the very familiar Schrodinger's-cat classroom bit and has the student's question genuinely complicate the thought experiment (the geiger counter as internal observer), giving the trope a new wrinkle.

criteria.name: Resonant closing image
criteria.instruction: Score whether the final line or image crystallizes the story’s central tension and adds meaning beyond simple stopping or surprise. Score high when the ending lingers and echoes earlier material; score low when it is generic, abrupt, or merely a disconnected punchline.
criteria.rationale: R03’s repeated service refrain gains new meaning after the death, and R31’s disappearance into the dream completes the protector’s role. R12 and R28 end on pleasant jokes that do not substantially deepen what came before.

criteria.name: Subtextual Character Conflict
criteria.instruction: Score high when desires, resentments, loyalties, or fears emerge through behavior and implication as well as dialogue; score low when characters simply announce flat motives or stereotypes.
criteria.rationale: R04 and R34 communicate conflicted loyalties through thought and action, unlike the largely declared emotional positions in R15 and R16.

criteria.name: Self-Contained Narrative Payoff
criteria.instruction: Score high when the presented text establishes enough context, completes a meaningful arc, and lands on an earned endpoint; score low when it depends on prior installments, promotional framing, moderation text, or an unresolved setup.
criteria.rationale: R03, R23, and R28 provide intelligible arcs within the excerpt, whereas R07, R25, R26, and R27 rely on meta-context, continuation, or failure to produce a complete story.

criteria.name: Sentence-level freshness vs. cliche phrasing
criteria.instruction: Score high if sentences contain apt, unexpected imagery or phrasing that couldn't be swapped into any other story. Score low if the prose leans on stock phrases and off-the-shelf genre diction ('dead meat,' 'evil clutches,' 'how dare you').
criteria.rationale: R18 repeatedly produces original figurative language ('eating the decorative swan at a banquet before it has had time to preen itself'), while R28 ('I'd just break theirs, physically') and R24 ('How dare you compare me... the audacity!') rely on generic, interchangeable genre phrasing.

criteria.name: Moral discomfort left standing, not resolved for the reader
criteria.instruction: Ask whether the story leaves the reader holding something unpleasant. CLEARLY SATISFYING: the piece commits to a perspective the reader cannot comfortably endorse -- a narrator whose reasoning is coherent and wrong, cruelty rendered without editorial distancing, an ending that refuses to adjudicate -- and does not supply a character or line that tells the reader how to feel. CLEARLY FAILING: the moral is stated, the transgressor is punished or reformed on cue, or a figure of authority appears to articulate the rules and the lesson. Judge refusal to resolve, not shock content: gore or profanity alone satisfies nothing.
criteria.rationale: R12 ends with the narrator's new hunger presented as pleasure, with no correction offered; R40 keeps its unrepentant murderer sympathetic to the last line; R07 lets an author torture his own creation for entertainment and signs off 'Well...that was fun :)'. All three are scorecard-low. The scorecard-high pole tidies up: R08's angel states 'We have rules' and the story delivers exact karmic symmetry, and R03 resolves its transgression into companionable warmth. Items rewarding thematic clarity and a satisfying resolution will systematically prefer the tidied version.

criteria.name: Selective Sensory Specificity
criteria.instruction: Score high when concrete sensory details are distinctive, selective, and reveal character, danger, or setting; score low when details are generic, ornamental, or piled on without function.
criteria.rationale: R03 and R24 use smell, texture, heat, and touch to deepen their situations, while R06 and R38 often accumulate descriptive details without comparable narrative leverage.

criteria.name: Earned recontextualization
criteria.instruction: Score whether a later revelation meaningfully changes the interpretation of earlier details and is prepared by prior evidence. Score high when the reversal feels inevitable in retrospect; score low when it is merely announced or appended at the end.
criteria.rationale: R05’s infection reveal transforms the narrator’s earlier testimony, and R30’s shifting domestic reality gradually exposes the coma. R09’s final testing message and R14’s final joke provide comparatively little preparation or reinterpretation.

criteria.name: Agency under constraint
criteria.instruction: Score whether the protagonist makes consequential choices despite meaningful limitations, and whether those choices alter the story. Score high when decisions reveal character and carry costs; score low when the protagonist mainly observes events or acts without changing the trajectory.
criteria.rationale: R02 makes Alfred’s scientific knowledge decisive, and R18’s fear and family duty force the rider into a dangerous choice. R13’s narrator is largely carried by confusion, while R17’s protagonist disappears before his own investigation can resolve.

criteria.name: Dramatized Exposition
criteria.instruction: Score high when necessary context is revealed through consequential action, conflict, or purposeful dialogue; score low when long explanatory passages delay the scene and could be removed without changing events.
criteria.rationale: R03, R21, and R39 disclose rules and history during immediate danger, whereas R05 and R40 front-load extensive explanation before meaningful dramatic movement.

criteria.name: Premise-to-Plot Transformation
criteria.instruction: Score high when the prompt's unusual element generates specific conflict, choices, and meaning; score low when it is merely mentioned or used as decorative genre dressing.
criteria.rationale: R14 and R24 make the speculative premise reshape the entire situation and worldview, whereas R01 and R25 barely develop their prompts.

criteria.name: Narrative economy
criteria.instruction: Score whether the story spends words on details that advance character, tension, setting, or theme. Score high when repetition and setup are purposeful; score low when boilerplate, promotion, recap, or redundant explanation displaces the story.
criteria.rationale: R16 creates a complete premise-and-ending arc in very few lines, while R35 moves efficiently from interrogation to reversal. R10 is almost entirely boilerplate, and R40 devotes substantial space to exposition before the immediate conflict.

criteria.name: Text is community apparatus rather than narrative
criteria.instruction: Score the fraction of the text that is subreddit machinery instead of story: explanations of how a recurring feature works, instructions about tagging or reposting, statements made in the first-person plural voice of the moderating body or an automated system, references to the subreddit's user base or rules. HIGH = the submission contains no fiction at all and reads as an announcement, notice, or procedural explainer. LOW = the text is wholly narrative with at most a short signature line.
criteria.upstream_parent: moderator and curation dynamics (author is staff, or the artefact is machine-generated by the platform)
criteria.rationale: R03 answers a [PI] prompt with several paragraphs explaining how the monthly Challenge the Mods feature runs, in the voice of the moderating team ('we have close to 13 million users'), and contains no story whatsoever; R30 is a verbatim automated removal notice instructing the poster to prefix their post with a two-letter tag. Both are institutional artefacts that entered the pool through curation rather than authorship, and both land at an extreme on at least one model. Being a moderator or an automod cannot make a piece of writing good, so any predictive power here is pure reception.

criteria.name: External-audience promotion
criteria.instruction: Count links, subreddit plugs, feedback requests, author tags, or invitations to read more; high means several such cues, low means none.
criteria.upstream_parent: established following, cross-posting, or social-network reach
criteria.rationale: These cues appear in R06, R15, R23, R25, R32, and R35. They can create a social-context signal without establishing story quality; an established following may also arise from genuinely experienced writing.

criteria.name: Explicit novice disclaimer or feedback solicitation
criteria.instruction: Score HIGH if the author explicitly states this is an early/first attempt at creative writing, or directly begs for critique/feedback in first person outside the fiction (e.g. 'first time ever writing...any criticism appreciated'). Score LOW if no such meta-commentary about the author's experience level or request for feedback appears.
criteria.upstream_parent: community norm of extending goodwill/leniency to self-identified newcomers -- the disclaimer itself invites sympathetic engagement independent of the prose
criteria.rationale: R02 ('This is actually my first time ever writing something...any genuine criticism to help me approve would be greatly appreciated') and R33 ('All crit/feedback welcome!') both solicit sympathy/engagement through explicit meta-appeal rather than through the writing itself.

criteria.name: Dialogue-first openings
criteria.instruction: Estimate the share of the opening passage occupied by dialogue and the number of turns before substantial narration appears. High means the story begins as rapid exchange; low means narration or description leads.
criteria.rationale: Fast conversational openings resemble familiar platform-native fiction formats and may invite an automatic stylistic reaction. R02 and R30 begin almost entirely as exchanges, as does R39's script-like presentation.

criteria.name: Serial continuity cues
criteria.instruction: Count explicit continuation notes, references to earlier installments, recurring-story framing, or next-stage hooks; high means substantial dependence on prior or future installments, low means self-contained framing.
criteria.rationale: R06 explicitly identifies itself as a continuation, while R40 closes with a staged experiment hook and extensive prior-event framing. Such cues can recruit familiarity with an ongoing story without proving quality; serial practice may also improve craft.

criteria.name: Editorial polish signature
criteria.instruction: Assess the consistency of spelling, punctuation, paragraphing, naming, and presentation across the visible text. High means publication-like regularity with few mechanical slips; low means conspicuous typos, dropped words, or inconsistent formatting.
criteria.rationale: External editing or professional experience can signal authority and can also genuinely improve prose, making this an intentionally mixed channel rather than a pure quality measure. R10 and R24 show highly controlled presentation, while R34 contains conspicuous mechanical slips.

criteria.name: Borrowed famous characters and pre-existing fictional worlds
criteria.instruction: Score how much of the story's furniture is imported from a work the reader is presumed to already know: named characters from an existing film, book, or series; an established setting with its own proper nouns and rules; recognisable catchphrases or signature props reproduced from the source. HIGH = the central figures and setting are all borrowed and the story relies on prior knowledge for its charge; MEDIUM = one borrowed figure in an original frame; LOW = wholly invented material.
criteria.upstream_parent: cross-posting and fandom audience overlap: the piece arrives with a readership that is already invested in the source
criteria.rationale: R08 puts a Coen-brothers killer with his coin toss and captive-bolt pistol in front of Joffrey Baratheon and lets the collision do the work; R23 runs on Hogwarts, Death Eaters and Lucius Malfoy, with invented mock-Latin spells doing the plotting; R29 places Freddy Krueger in a child's bedroom and relies entirely on the reader knowing who has the fingerblades. In each case a large share of the reader's investment is pre-loaded by the source rather than earned by the page, and I mark mixed false because borrowing a famous character supplies recognition without supplying any craft the writer did not already have.

criteria.name: Explicit tournament/contest round or heat marker
criteria.instruction: Score HIGH if the prompt or story text names a structured competitive format -- round/heat numbering (e.g. 'Round 1 Heat 30'), bracket-style language ('congratulations to everyone who...got through'), or an explicit elimination/advancement frame. Score LOW if the piece is a standalone response with no bracket/round language.
criteria.upstream_parent: participation in a structured bracket-style contest thread -- voting in these threads is shaped by advancement stakes and voting blocs, not the entry's standalone merit
criteria.rationale: R34 (titled '20/20 Round 1 Heat 30', closing note about 'everyone who participated...got through') and R24 (tagged [IP], the same tournament format) both carry this bracket signature; tournament rounds create strategic/allegiance voting dynamics unrelated to prose quality.

criteria.name: Dialogue punctuation mark count
criteria.instruction: Count how many quotation marks (" or “”) the story contains. Score 1.0 when quotation marks are very numerous, 0.5 when there are a few, 0.0 when there are none. Count the punctuation only; pay no attention to whether any speech is well written or whether the voices differ.
criteria.rationale: PLANTED PROBE (coordinator-authored). Shallow typographic counterpart of R2A01 'Character-specific voice': quotation-mark density is the surface trace of dialogue and therefore correlates with voice work, while measuring nothing about whether different characters sound different. A competent blind auditor should route this probe to the nuisance side and R2A01 to the bank.

criteria.name: Final-paragraph word count
criteria.instruction: Count the words in the story's last paragraph. Score 1.0 when the last paragraph is very short (under about fifteen words), 0.5 when it is of ordinary length, 0.0 when it is long. Count the words only; pay no attention to what the last paragraph says or whether it lands.
criteria.rationale: PLANTED PROBE (coordinator-authored). Shallow length counterpart of R2A05 'Resonant closing image': a short final paragraph is the typographic signature of a punchy ending, while measuring nothing about whether the closing image resonates.
